items.readable_text:
Content:
Logical operations with predicates generalize the corresponding operations on statements. As a result, all the properties of these operations are held.

Content:
In particular, for predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),] De Morgan's laws state the following:

Content:
[MATH: ¬(P∧Q)|≡¬P∨¬Q; ¬(P∨Q)|≡¬P∧¬Q]

Content:
These can be used to negate open sentences containing conjunctions and disjunctions. For example, let's negate the following:

Content:
[MATH: n \ge 0 \:\textbf{ or }\: 2 \mid m]

Content:
Applying De Morgan's law for disjunctions, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ¬(n ≥ 0or2∣m)|≡¬(n ≥ 0∨2∣m); ≡¬(n ≥ 0)∧¬(2∣m); ≡n < 0∧2∤m; ≡n < 0and2∤m.]

  • [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is greater than [MATH: 4]

  • [MATH: Q(x):] [MATH: x] is rational

items.title: Negating a Conjunction Using De Morgan's Law

sections.normalized_html:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: x] is prime and [MATH: y] divides [MATH: 12].

What is the negation of the composite predicate above?
sections.readable_text:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: x] is prime and [MATH: y] divides [MATH: 12].

What is the negation of the composite predicate above?

sections.normalized_html:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

[MATH: eg ( A \land B) = eg A \lor eg B.]

So, the negation of "[MATH: x] is prime and [MATH: y] divides [MATH: 12]" is

[MATH: ¬(xis prime andydivides12)|≡¬(xis prime∧ydivides12); ≡¬(xis prime)∨¬(ydivides12); ≡xis not prime∨ydoes not divide12; ≡xis not primeorydoes not divide12.]
sections.readable_text:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

[MATH: \neg ( A \land B) = \neg A \lor \neg B.]

So, the negation of "[MATH: x] is prime and [MATH: y] divides [MATH: 12]" is

[MATH: ¬(xis prime andydivides12)|≡¬(xis prime∧ydivides12); ≡¬(xis prime)∨¬(ydivides12); ≡xis not prime∨ydoes not divide12; ≡xis not primeorydoes not divide12.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Logical operations with predicates generalize the corresponding operations on statements. As a result, all the properties of these operations are held.

Content:
In particular, for predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),] De Morgan's laws state the following:

Content:
[MATH: ¬(P∧Q)|≡¬P∨¬Q; ¬(P∨Q)|≡¬P∧¬Q]

Content:
These can be used to negate open sentences containing conjunctions and disjunctions. For example, let's negate the following:

Content:
[MATH: n \ge 0 \:\textbf{ or }\: 2 \mid m]

Content:
Applying De Morgan's law for disjunctions, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ¬(n ≥ 0or2∣m)|≡¬(n ≥ 0∨2∣m); ≡¬(n ≥ 0)∧¬(2∣m); ≡n < 0∧2∤m; ≡n < 0and2∤m.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Expressing a Predicate in Symbolic Form

Example Prompt:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: x] is greater than [MATH: 4,] or [MATH: x] is irrational.

Express the compound predicate above in symbolic form given the following predicates:

- [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is greater than [MATH: 4]
- [MATH: Q(x):] [MATH: x] is rational

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The sentence

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: x] is irrational

can be expressed in symbolic form as [MATH: \lnot Q.]

Therefore, the given sentence is expressed symbolically as
[MATH: P\lor \lnot Q.]

What is the negation of the composite predicate above?
